lessons.title: Context: Caribbean Immigration & British Identity
lessons.description: Winsome Pinnock, the Windrush generation and the 1980s context behind Leave Taking.
lessons.content_html:
Winsome Pinnock and Leave Taking

Leave Taking (1987) by Winsome Pinnock is a play about a Caribbean-British family navigating questions of identity, belonging and cultural roots in 1984 London. For AQA your second exam paper, you study it as a modern drama text. The play focuses on Enid Matthews, a Jamaican-born mother raising two daughters (Del and Viv) in England, and her complex relationship with Mai — an Obeah woman who represents the Caribbean spiritual traditions Enid has tried to leave behind.

Key Fact

Pinnock was one of the first Black British women playwrights to have work staged in major London theatres. Leave Taking draws on the Windrush generation experience — Caribbean immigrants who came to Britain seeking a better life but faced racism, cultural displacement and the challenge of raising children between two worlds.

Historical Context

After World War II, Britain actively recruited workers from the Caribbean. The British Nationality Act 1948 gave them the right to settle. The HMT Empire Windrush brought the first large group in 1948. By 1984, when the play is set, the children of these immigrants were growing up British but facing racism and questions about where they truly belonged. The 1981 Brixton riots and the 1971 Immigration Act form part of the backdrop to the racial tensions Enid’s family navigates.

Pinnock is part of a tradition of Black British theatre that emerged in the 1980s, giving voice to experiences largely absent from mainstream stages. Leave Taking is significant because it centres Caribbean-British women’s experiences — motherhood, cultural identity, generational conflict — rather than presenting them as secondary to male or white narratives. When the National Theatre produced the play in 1994, it was the first time a Black British woman’s play had been staged there — a historic milestone. The 2018 Bush Theatre revival, directed by Madani Younis, introduced the play to a new generation.

The Play’s Two Settings

Leave Taking is set in 1984 London and is structured as eight scenes — not two formal acts. The play has two physical settings: Enid’s North London living room (Scenes 2–5) and Mai’s Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8). The play opens and closes at Mai’s bedsit — the Caribbean spiritual space frames the entire action. This is structurally significant: the domestic English space is bracketed by the world of Obeah and Caribbean roots, suggesting that Enid’s attempt to confine her family to English respectability is always surrounded by the heritage she tried to suppress.

Key Fact

Scene 1 takes place on Easter Monday, 1984, at Mai’s Deptford bedsit. Enid brings both daughters there for a reading. Del stays behind when Enid and Viv leave. The play’s final scene (Scene 8) also takes place at Mai’s bedsit — where Del reads Enid’s palm as Mai’s spiritual successor. The Caribbean space opens and closes the play, framing the family’s journey.

The first generation of Caribbean immigrants faced a painful dilemma: to survive in a racist Britain, many felt they had to suppress their cultural identity, language and spiritual practices. The cost of this strategy fell on the second generation, who grew up in England but felt culturally rootless. They were too English for Jamaica, but not fully accepted in England. Pinnock’s play dramatises this dilemma through Enid (first generation) and her daughters Del and Viv (second generation). The tension between assimilation and cultural belonging is the engine of the entire play.

Context and Critical Reception

Understanding the social and historical context in which a play was written is essential for top-band exam responses. For Leave Taking, this means engaging with the experience of the Windrush generation and the particular challenges facing Black British women in the 1980s. Winsome Pinnock brings her own background to the play, writing from within a community whose stories had been largely absent from mainstream British theatre. The play's critical reception has grown over time: the 1994 National Theatre production was historic, and the 2018 Bush Theatre revival confirmed its status as a landmark text in British drama. When writing about the play, always connect the specific scene or character detail you are analysing to this broader context — explaining not just what Pinnock shows, but why she chose to show it.

lessons.title: Scenes 1–3: Enid, Del & the Obeah Woman
lessons.description: Scene 1 at Mai's bedsit, the sisters' contrasting characters, and Enid's mother's death in Scene 3.
lessons.content_html:
Enid's World

The play's opening scenes introduce Enid Matthews, a Jamaican-born mother who has built a life in London through hard work and sacrifice. She works long hours — as a hospital cleaner, sometimes at two jobs — to provide for her daughters, Del and Viv, and is determined that they will succeed through education and respectability. Enid has deliberately distanced herself from her Caribbean roots: she rarely speaks about Jamaica and dismisses traditional practices as backward. Pinnock presents Enid as a woman whose survival strategy is assimilation — she believes that fitting into English society is the best way to protect her daughters.

Key Fact

Enid's rejection of her Caribbean heritage is born from experience, not indifference. She believes that respectability and English education will protect her daughters from the racism she has experienced. But this strategy creates a painful gap between Enid and her cultural identity — and between Enid and her daughters, who sense a heritage they cannot name.

Del and Viv

Del (Delores) is the elder daughter, aged 18. She is rebellious and instinctive — she stays out late, loses her job after arguing with her manager, and is drawn to Mai and the world of Obeah. Viv (Vivienne) is the younger daughter, aged 17, and is academically focused: she is preparing for her A-level exams and plans eventually to study at university. The sisters represent two responses to the immigrant experience — Del's resistance to assimilation and Viv's apparent conformity — but Pinnock complicates both positions as the play develops.

Scene 1 takes place at Mai's Deptford bedsit on Easter Monday. Enid brings both daughters to Mai for a reading — her stated concern is about a letter she received from her sister Cynthia in Jamaica saying that their mother is seriously ill and asking for money. Enid suspects her sister may be exaggerating to extract funds, but Mai advises her to send the money anyway. Enid's other worry — which she shares cautiously — is about Del's behaviour. Del stays behind at Mai's bedsit when Enid and Viv leave. This opening scene establishes the play's two settings and the pull that Mai's Caribbean world exerts on Del.

Mai: The Obeah Woman

Mai is a practitioner of Obeah — Caribbean folk magic rooted in West African spiritual traditions. She lives in a Deptford bedsit, physically declining but spiritually authoritative. She represents everything Enid has tried to leave behind: Jamaica, the old ways, spiritual belief systems that do not fit into English respectability. Mai's presence connects the family to their cultural roots, offering an alternative to Enid's strategy of assimilation. She recognises Del's potential as her spiritual successor from the start.

Brod (Broderick) is Enid's long-standing friend, a fellow Windrush-generation Jamaican who is present throughout key scenes — most significantly Scenes 2, 3 and 7. He is the play's only significant male character and provides a counterpoint to Enid's resilience. Brod has a serious drinking problem, has lost contact with his children, and is deeply disenchanted with life in England. He embodies a Windrush experience that Enid has refused to allow herself: the disillusionment of a man who gave up everything for a country that never fully accepted him.

Scene 3: Enid's Mother Dies

The emotional turning point of the play's first half comes in Scene 3, when Enid learns that her mother has died in Jamaica. The news arrives via another letter — confirming what Enid had feared and half-denied since Scene 1. This is not a simple bereavement: Enid's relationship with her mother was strained. Her mother called her 'Miss English', mocking Enid's assimilation. Enid sent money home but kept her distance — both geographically and emotionally. The death of her mother therefore carries grief compounded by guilt, estrangement and the knowledge that the relationship can never now be repaired.

Key Fact

Enid's emotional collapse after her mother's death in Scene 3 is the play's first major crisis. It cracks open the composure Enid has maintained through assimilation. Her grief is not simply about her mother's death — it is about everything she left behind in Jamaica: her roots, her language, the life she might have had. Pinnock uses this bereavement to humanise Enid and to begin the process by which she is gradually forced to reconnect with what she suppressed.

lessons.title: Scenes 4–7: Generational Conflict
lessons.description: Del moves to Mai's, Del's pregnancy, Viv's exam rebellion, and Brod's revelation about the abusive father.
lessons.content_html:
The Crises Converge

In Scenes 4–7, the tensions established in the opening scenes crack open into genuine crisis. Three parallel developments drive this section: Del deepens her relationship with Mai and eventually moves into her Deptford bedsit; Del's pregnancy becomes apparent; and Viv, the apparently conformist daughter, begins to rebel in her own way — walking out of one of her A-level exams. Pinnock uses these parallel crises to show that Enid's strategy of assimilation cannot contain the complexity of her daughters' lives, and that both sisters ultimately reject the identity their mother has tried to impose on them — just in different ways.

Key Fact

Del's pregnancy belongs to Del, the elder daughter (18) — not to Viv. Enid's worry about Del in Scene 1, when she first visits Mai, is later confirmed: Del is indeed pregnant, the father absent. This is one of the play's major plot developments. Viv's parallel crisis is entirely different — it is educational and intellectual, not physical.

Del and Mai

Del's relationship with Mai intensifies across these scenes. Initially Enid brought Del to Mai hoping Mai might help control her — but Del becomes Mai's ally and eventual successor instead. Del discovers she is dyslexic, which reframes her difficulties at school: she was not lazy or rebellious in failing to engage with formal education — she was struggling with a barrier that the school system never identified. Del moves out of Enid's home and into Mai's bedsit, a decision that causes Enid enormous distress. But Mai recognises Del's potential as a healer and spiritual practitioner, and begins to train her.

Del becomes pregnant during this section of the play. The father is absent. This development is dramatically significant because it confirms Enid's original fear from Scene 1 (her worry about Del's behaviour was partly a worry about this) and because it places Del in a position of vulnerability at exactly the moment she is finding her own path through Mai. Pinnock does not present the pregnancy as a catastrophe — it is one of several things Del must navigate as she builds an identity independent of both Enid's expectations and conventional English society.

Viv's Rebellion

Viv's crisis is very different from Del's — it takes place in her head and in the exam hall rather than in the streets or at Mai's bedsit. In Scene 5, Viv walks out of one of her A-level exams. This is not impulsiveness: it reflects a growing crisis of identity that Viv has been suppressing alongside her studies. Viv's complaint is that the education system does not reflect her experience or heritage. She feels invisible within it — a student whose culture is absent from the curriculum she is being tested on. She has worked hard for an education that, she is beginning to realise, does not fully include her.

Key Fact

Viv's rebellion is intellectual and cultural, not romantic or physical. After walking out of the exam, she determines to study Black Studies at university — a subject that actually includes her experience. She says something close to: no matter how hard I search for myself in these books, I am never there. This is not a rejection of education — it is a rejection of a Eurocentric education that treats her heritage as invisible.

Scene 7: Brod Tells Del the Truth

Scene 7, set at Mai's bedsit, contains one of the play's most important revelations. Brod — Enid's Windrush-generation friend — tells Del the truth about her father. Enid's husband was abusive. He subjected Enid to domestic violence. The racism he suffered at work — described by Brod as relentless and dehumanising — made him hard and cruel, turning him into someone who took out his degradation on the person closest to him. Enid eventually left him, but she never told her daughters the truth about why.

This revelation is crucial for understanding Enid's character. Her fierce protectiveness and controlling behaviour are not simply about cultural ambition or snobbery — they come from a woman who survived abuse and displacement and is determined that her daughters will not experience the same. The revelation also illuminates Brod's disillusionment: he, too, has watched the Windrush promise of a better life corroded by racism and poverty. Brod describes a friend — Gullyman — who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown. England's racism, Pinnock suggests, spares no one.

By Scene 6, Enid herself comes to Mai's bedsit — searching for Del, but also, Pinnock suggests, beginning to seek healing she cannot articulate. Mai reads Enid's palm and tells her she will make a long journey. This prediction introduces the possibility of reconciliation and reconnection that the final scene will deliver. Mai is physically declining throughout these scenes — she nearly faints at one point — and it is clear she is dying. But she uses what life remains to ensure Del is ready to inherit her role.

lessons.title: Resolution & the Ending
lessons.description: Del reads Enid's palm, Mai's departure, Viv leaves for university, and the play's fragile reconciliation.
lessons.content_html:
Scene 8: The Final Confrontation

Leave Taking's final scene takes place at Mai's Deptford bedsit — the same space in which the play opened. The return to this setting is structurally deliberate: the Caribbean spiritual world, which Enid tried to exclude from her family's life, has not been left behind. It is the space in which the family's most important reckoning takes place. The confrontation that scene 8 brings is raw, painful and deeply human: Enid must face what she has suppressed, Del must choose whether to allow Enid back into her life, and Viv must prepare for her departure to university.

Pinnock stages this confrontation not as melodrama but as messy, overlapping domestic reality: raised voices, tears, silences, accusations that carry weight because they contain truth. Enid is forced to confront the cost of her strategy of suppression — she cannot control Del's choices, she cannot prevent grief or loss, and she cannot maintain the silence that has defined her relationship with her own history.

Key Fact

Pinnock's naturalistic dialogue in Scene 8 — characters interrupting each other, retreating, returning — reflects how real families argue about real pain. The authenticity deepens the emotional impact: the audience feels they are witnessing something genuine rather than scripted. This is a deliberate dramatic choice — the absence of melodrama makes the reconciliation feel hard-won rather than inevitable.

Del Reads Enid's Palm

The play's most powerful moment comes when Del reads Enid's palm. This is the play's emotional climax and its central symbolic act. Mai, who is dying, has given Del her notebook — the accumulated knowledge of an Obeah woman — and has left Del with Enid as her first 'client'. Del performing the palm reading she once refused (in Scene 1 she declined to have her own palm read) signals her transformation: she has accepted her gift, accepted Mai's inheritance, and accepted a version of herself that has room for both her Caribbean heritage and her English present.

The palm reading is also a gesture of reconciliation towards Enid. Del is not simply performing a spiritual act — she is offering her mother something: acknowledgement, connection, a bridge across the distance that Enid's assimilation strategy created. Enid, who dismissed Mai's Obeah as backward, allows her daughter to read her palm. This is Enid's own act of acceptance — small, tentative, but real.

Pinnock places two candles on stage in Scene 8. A half-burnt white candle sits near Mai — her life and role ending. A fully-lit candle sits in front of Del — her life and role beginning. This stagecraft encapsulates the play's central movement: a spiritual inheritance passing from one generation to the next. Mai is not simply dying — she is completing a task. Del is not simply surviving her chaotic adolescence — she is beginning something.

Fragile Reconciliation and the Title's Meanings

The title 'Leave Taking' comes full circle in Scene 8. It carries at least three meanings that the ending makes explicit. First, Enid's original leave-taking: her departure from Jamaica — and from her mother, from her roots — that created the displacement the family has been living with. Second, the daughters' leave-taking: Del leaving Enid's home to live at Mai's; Viv departing for university and a future Enid did not plan for her. Third — and most importantly — the leave-taking from shame: letting go of the secrecy and self-denial that defined Enid's relationship with her heritage.

Key Fact

Pinnock's most radical message is that cultural identity can be reclaimed even after years of suppression. The ending suggests that it is never too late to reconnect with one's roots — not by going back to Jamaica, but by acknowledging Jamaica's presence in who you are. This message mirrors the real experience of many second- and third-generation immigrant families rediscovering the heritage their parents or grandparents suppressed.

Leave Taking's ending offers fragile reconciliation rather than a neat happy ending. Pinnock does not pretend that one conversation can undo decades of suppression. Enid's grief about her mother's death cannot be erased. The racism that drove her assimilation has not disappeared. Del has not returned home — she stays at Mai's bedsit with her pregnancy and her new role. But there is movement: a willingness to be honest, to accept what was previously denied, to hold complexity rather than demand simplicity.

The 2018 Bush Theatre revival of Leave Taking demonstrates the play's continued relevance. Thirty years after it was written, the questions it asks — Where do I belong? What did my parents sacrifice? How do I hold two cultures at once? — remain urgently alive for Caribbean-British families and for immigrant communities more broadly.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Character analysis of Enid Matthews, Del, and Mai — their methods, motivations and roles in the play.
lessons.content_html:
Enid Matthews

Enid is the play's central character — the person whose choices, fears and history drive the action. She is a first-generation Jamaican immigrant who came to England around 1959 as part of the Windrush generation. She works as a hospital cleaner — sometimes at two jobs simultaneously — and has devoted her life to her daughters' security. Enid's defining strategy is assimilation: she speaks 'proper' English, dismisses Obeah as superstition, and suppresses any reference to Jamaican culture that might mark her daughters as outsiders.

Enid's backstory is gradually revealed across the play. Her husband subjected her to domestic violence — cruelty rooted in the racism and humiliation he suffered at work — and Enid ended the marriage to protect her daughters. Brod discloses this to Del in Scene 7, overturning the assumption Del has carried for years that her mother drove her father away. Enid's mother called her 'Miss English' and the two became estranged; Enid sent money home but kept emotional distance. When her mother dies in Scene 3, Enid's grief is compounded by the estrangement that can never now be resolved. Her controlling behaviour is not cruelty — it is a survivor's response to racism, poverty, abuse and loss.

Key Fact

Enid's controlling behaviour has three roots: (1) her abusive marriage — she will not allow her daughters to experience what she endured; (2) her mother's death and their estranged relationship — she cannot bear to lose her daughters the same way; (3) her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant — she believes assimilation is the only protection she can offer. Understanding these three drivers is essential for top-band analysis.

Del (Delores)

Del is the elder daughter, aged 18. She is the play's most instinctive character — rebellious, sensory, drawn to things she cannot fully articulate. She stays out late, loses her job after arguing with her manager, and initially refuses to have her palm read by Mai. But she is drawn irresistibly to Mai's world. She later discovers she is dyslexic, which reframes her educational struggles: she was not lazy but struggling with an undiagnosed barrier. She becomes pregnant — the father absent — and eventually moves into Mai's Deptford bedsit, beginning her training as Mai's spiritual successor.

By the final scene, Del has been transformed. She reads Enid's palm — a spiritual act she once refused — and in doing so offers Enid the bridge to her own heritage that Enid could never build alone. Del's arc is about discovering her true identity: not the respectable English daughter Enid wanted, and not simply a rebellious teenager, but someone with a genuine gift and a genuine heritage to inhabit.

Viv is the younger daughter, aged 17. She appears to be Enid's success story: educated, articulate, preparing for A-level exams. She has adopted English culture more fully than Del and seems comfortable in it. But Pinnock complicates this apparent conformity through Viv's educational rebellion. She walks out of one of her exams — an act of defiance against a Eurocentric curriculum that, she says, has no place for her. She feels invisible within it: 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.' She plans to study Black Studies at university — a subject that acknowledges her existence — and the play ends with her leaving for precisely that future.

Viv's rebellion is intellectual rather than physical. Her crisis is not a pregnancy or a departure from home but a crisis of educational identity — a recognition that the path Enid mapped for her was built on a curriculum that erased her. Both daughters ultimately reject Enid's assimilation strategy, but they do so in ways that reflect their different personalities.

Mai

Mai is an Obeah woman who lives in a Deptford bedsit. She is physically declining throughout the play — nearly fainting at one point, clearly dying by the end — but her spiritual authority is undiminished. She has an estranged adult son. She charges no fee for Enid's final reading, out of sympathy. Pinnock presents Mai not as superstition to be overcome but as a figure of genuine wisdom and cultural continuity. She sees clearly what each character needs: Del needs to be recognised as a healer; Enid needs permission to reconnect with what she suppressed. Mai does not impose — she offers.

Brod is Enid's childhood friend from Jamaica, a fellow Windrush immigrant. He appears on stage in Scenes 2, 3 and 7 — he is not an absent or offstage character. He has a serious drinking problem, has children he no longer sees, and is deeply disenchanted with life in England. He describes a friend, Gullyman, who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown — arguing that England's racism corrodes everyone eventually, however successful they appear.

Brod's most important dramatic function is in Scene 7, when he tells Del about her father's abusive treatment of Enid and about the racism that drove it. He is the only character who can deliver this truth — not because he is wise, but because he was there. Pinnock uses Brod to show that the truth about the past must eventually be spoken, even if imperfectly, by imperfect people.

Key Fact

Understanding the playwright's specific choices — structure, language, staging and context — is essential for top-band analysis. Make sure you can discuss how form and content work together to create meaning for the audience.

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

lessons.title: Structure & Stagecraft
lessons.description: Eight-scene structure, dual settings, domestic realism, Obeah and Pinnock's stagecraft choices.
lessons.content_html:
Eight Scenes: The Play's Structure

Leave Taking is structured as eight scenes, not two formally titled acts. This is how it appears in the published Nick Hern Books text and how it is organised in performance. In analysis and exam responses, you should refer to 'Scene 1', 'Scene 7' and so on, rather than 'Act 1' or 'Act 2', to be precise about the text you are studying. There is a structural shift roughly in the middle of the play — the first four scenes establishing tension, the second four escalating into crisis and resolution — but this is a structural pattern, not a formal act division.

The pacing across the eight scenes is deliberate: Scenes 1–5 are slower, domestic, built around everyday tensions — arguments about respectability, education, money, the letter from Jamaica. Scenes 6–8 accelerate as crises converge — Del at Mai's, Enid searching for her, Brod's revelation, and the final reconciliation. This structural contrast mirrors the family's experience: years of quiet suppression followed by a crisis that forces everything into the open.

Key Fact

Pinnock's choice to build the early scenes around domestic routine before cracking it open in the later scenes reflects the real experience of immigrant families: cultural conflict often simmers beneath the surface of ordinary life for years before a crisis forces it into the open. The structure of the play is part of Pinnock's argument.

Dual Settings: Two Physical Spaces

Leave Taking has two distinct physical settings. Enid's North London living room appears in Scenes 2–5: the domestic English space, defined by routine, respectability and suppression. Mai's Deptford bedsit appears in Scenes 1, 6, 7 and 8: the Caribbean spiritual space, associated with Obeah, cultural roots and healing. Crucially, the play opens at Mai's bedsit (Scene 1) and ends there (Scene 8). This means the Caribbean spiritual world frames the entire action — it is where the story begins and where it is resolved.

Pinnock's staging of two physical settings is itself a structural statement. Enid's home is the space she controls; Mai's bedsit is the space Enid cannot control. Del gravitates from one to the other across the play. The final resolution can only happen at Mai's — not in Enid's living room. This tells us something about what the play argues: the family cannot heal in the space built on suppression; they must go to the space built on honesty.

Leave Taking is written in a domestic realist style for much of its length. The dialogue sounds like real speech: overlapping, interrupted, emotionally loaded. Characters argue about tea, homework, clothes and money — the fabric of ordinary domestic life. Pinnock uses this realism to show that the play's grand themes (identity, belonging, cultural displacement) are not abstract but lived in every meal, every conversation, every loaded silence. The domestic setting is not a backdrop — it is where culture is fought over.

Obeah: Breaking Realism

While the play is predominantly naturalistic, Mai's Obeah practice introduces a spiritual dimension that complicates the realism. When Mai performs rituals, reads palms or speaks of the spirit world, the language becomes more poetic and the atmosphere more charged. Pinnock does not present Obeah as superstition to be mocked; she treats it as a legitimate cultural practice with real power and real wisdom.

This structural tension between domestic realism and the spirit world is itself thematic. Enid has tried to live entirely in the 'rational' English world, rejecting Caribbean spirituality. Mai's presence reintroduces the spiritual dimension Enid suppressed. The play's hybrid form — realism interrupted by spirituality — mirrors the dual cultural identity the characters are navigating. You cannot fully separate the two registers any more than the characters can fully separate their two cultural identities.

Pinnock builds dramatic tension through gradual revelation. Enid's backstory — the abusive marriage, the estrangement from her mother, the shame about her Jamaican roots — is revealed in pieces across the play rather than in a single dramatic disclosure. Del's pregnancy is also revealed gradually. This technique of foreshadowing engages the audience as active interpreters, rewarding close attention to dialogue and behaviour. In Scene 1 we already know something is wrong before we understand exactly what.

The parallel crises of Del's pregnancy and Viv's exam rebellion create structural echoes: both daughters find their own way of refusing the identity Enid designed for them. This parallelism deepens the play's exploration of intergenerational patterns — the daughters are not simply rebelling but finding themselves.

For AQA Paper 2, discussing Pinnock's structural and staging choices is essential AO2 material. The eight-scene structure, the two physical settings, domestic realism, the hybrid incorporation of Obeah, and the technique of gradual revelation are all deliberate choices that shape meaning. Always explain why Pinnock makes these choices, not just that she does.

Key Fact

Understanding the playwright's specific choices — structure, language, staging and context — is essential for top-band analysis. Make sure you can discuss how form and content work together to create meaning for the audience.

lessons.title: Language, Dialect & Identity
lessons.description: Code-switching, Jamaican patois, generational voice and silence as dramatic tools in Leave Taking.
lessons.content_html:
Language as Identity

In Leave Taking, language is not just a medium of communication — it is a marker of identity. The way each character speaks reveals where they position themselves on the spectrum between Caribbean and English culture. Pinnock uses language consciously as a dramatic tool: the rhythms, vocabulary and patterns of each character's speech embody their relationship with cultural identity. For AQA Paper 2, this is rich AO2 material — language choices are deliberate methods through which Pinnock explores her themes.

Key Fact

Enid speaks predominantly in standard English — the language of assimilation. She has deliberately cultivated a 'respectable' way of speaking that signals her integration into English society. But when she is emotional, stressed or speaking about Jamaica, her language shifts: Jamaican patois breaks through the English surface. These moments of linguistic slippage are dramatically powerful because they reveal the Caribbean identity Enid has worked so hard to suppress.

Code-Switching

Code-switching is central to the play's linguistic texture. Enid code-switches unconsciously when her emotional defences are down — her patois emerging under pressure. Mai speaks with a stronger Jamaican register throughout, reflecting her uncompromised connection to Caribbean culture. Viv speaks almost entirely in standard London English, reflecting her deep assimilation. Del falls between: she can speak standard English but is increasingly drawn to Jamaican patterns through her relationship with Mai.

Pinnock's use of code-switching serves multiple functions. It is characterisation: each character's speech pattern reveals their cultural position. It is thematic: the tension between patois and standard English mirrors the broader tension between Caribbean heritage and English assimilation. And it is dramatic: when Enid's patois breaks through, the audience hears the identity she has been suppressing, creating powerful moments of revelation.

Jamaican patois (also called Jamaican Creole) is a full language with its own grammar, vocabulary and rhythm. It is not 'broken English' — it is a distinct linguistic system. Pinnock's inclusion of patois in the play is a political act as well as an artistic one: it insists that Caribbean language is valid, expressive and worthy of the stage. Mai's speech is richest in patois patterns, warm, rhythmic and proverbial. Her way of speaking carries the cadences of Jamaica — the oral traditions, the storytelling, the spiritual language of Obeah.

Standard English in the play represents the dominant culture. Enid's adoption of it is a conscious choice to be taken seriously in a society that marginalises Caribbean speakers. But the play shows that this choice has a cost: in gaining English respectability, Enid has lost the linguistic connection to her heritage. Her standard English is a kind of performance — and when the performance slips, the audience glimpses the woman underneath.

Generational Voice

The generational voice in Leave Taking is a key structural element. Enid's language sits between Jamaica and England — she can speak both but has chosen English dominance. Viv has almost entirely adopted London speech patterns: she sounds English in a way Enid never quite does. Del is the most linguistically fluid: she speaks English by default but absorbs Jamaican rhythms through Mai, becoming a bridge between the two worlds.

This generational progression — from patois-inflected English (Enid) to fully English (Viv) to consciously reclaiming patois (Del) — mirrors the broader pattern of immigrant linguistic experience. The first generation compromises; the second generation assimilates; the third generation often seeks to reconnect with the language their grandparents spoke. Pinnock captures this entire arc within a single family.

Key Fact

Language in Leave Taking is never neutral. Every word choice is a statement about identity. When Enid corrects Del's speech or insists on 'proper' English, she is performing her assimilation strategy through language. When Del absorbs Mai's Jamaican rhythms, she is reclaiming the heritage her mother suppressed. The play's dialogue is itself a cultural battleground.

Pinnock also uses silence as a dramatic tool. Enid's refusal to talk about Jamaica, her evasions when Del asks about their heritage, the long pauses when painful topics arise — these silences communicate as powerfully as speech. What Enid will not say is as revealing as what she does say. The gap between speech and silence maps the gap between her English surface and her Jamaican interior.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Belonging, cultural identity, motherhood, the generational divide, racism and AQA exam strategy.
lessons.content_html:
Theme 1: Belonging and Cultural Identity

Belonging is the play's central concern, and Pinnock argues that it requires accepting all parts of one's heritage — not choosing between Caribbean and English but holding both. Every character in Leave Taking struggles with where they belong. Enid belongs to neither Jamaica (which she left) nor England (which has never fully accepted her). Viv belongs in England linguistically and educationally but not emotionally. Del senses she belongs to a Caribbean heritage she has never directly experienced. Mai belongs fully to her Caribbean identity but is marginalised in English society.

Pinnock's resolution — fragile reconciliation rather than a neat happy ending — suggests that belonging is not a destination but a process. The family begins to hold both worlds without seeing them as contradictory. This is the play's most hopeful and most radical idea: hybrid identity is not a weakness but a strength.

Key Fact

The title 'Leave Taking' itself captures the theme of belonging. It refers to Enid's departure from Jamaica, the daughters' gradual departure from their mother's values, and — most importantly — the leave-taking from shame. Pinnock argues that immigrant families can only belong when they stop trying to leave their heritage behind.

Theme 2: Motherhood and Sacrifice

Motherhood runs through every strand of the play. Enid's motherhood is defined by sacrifice: she works exhausting hours, suppresses her own cultural identity and controls every aspect of her daughters' lives — all to give them a 'better' future. Her fierce protectiveness is driven by three things: her experience of an abusive marriage (she will not let her daughters be vulnerable), her mother's death and their estrangement (she cannot bear to lose her daughters the same way), and her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant. Del's pregnancy introduces a new generation of the motherhood theme, and by the final scene Del has also become a kind of mother-figure-in-waiting — Mai's successor and Enid's bridge back to heritage.

The generational divide between Enid and her daughters mirrors the broader Windrush experience. The first generation sacrificed everything — homeland, culture, identity — to build a life in England. The second generation, born in England, questions the cost of that sacrifice: Why did you suppress our heritage? Why can't we talk about Jamaica? What are you hiding? Pinnock shows both sides with sympathy: Enid's suppression comes from love, not malice, but it has created a void in her daughters' sense of self.

Crucially, Pinnock does not simply blame the older generation. She shows that Enid's choices were made in response to real racism and real economic hardship. The generational divide is not about one side being right — it is about understanding why each generation made the choices it did. This nuance is essential for top-band responses.

Racism is the backdrop against which every other theme plays out. Enid's assimilation is a response to racism. Mai's marginalisation reflects how Caribbean culture is dismissed by mainstream English society. Viv's sense of invisibility in the curriculum comes from a society that treats her heritage as inferior. Brod's disillusionment — and his account of how racism destroyed Del's father — shows the long-term human cost. Pinnock does not stage dramatic racist incidents: racism operates as a pervasive structural pressure shaping every character's choices. This is more realistic and more powerful.

AQA Exam Strategy

For AQA Paper 2, you will have a printed extract from Leave Taking. You may be asked to write about a theme, a character, or a dramatic method, drawing on both the extract and the whole play. Both tasks reward AO1 (personal response), AO2 (methods) and AO3 (context). Plan carefully, divide your time, and always check the specimen paper for the current question format.

Key Fact

Key quotations and moments to prepare: Enid's insistence on 'proper' English; her grief after her mother's death in Scene 3; Brod's revelation about the abusive father in Scene 7; Del moving to Mai's bedsit; Viv walking out of her exam; Del reading Enid's palm in Scene 8; the candle symbolism; the domestic setting as cultural battleground; the fragile reconciliation. Having 8–10 prepared areas — each connected to theme, character and method — allows you to adapt to any question.

Extract analysis strategy: Work through the extract methodically — identify Pinnock's key language choices, dramatic techniques and structural decisions. Quote precisely from the printed passage. For every technique, explain its effect on the audience and connect it to the question's focus.

Whole-play strategy: Range across the whole play — draw examples from across all eight scenes. Remember Leave Taking is a play: analyse dramatic techniques (naturalistic dialogue, code-switching, dual settings, Obeah scenes, silence, stagecraft) alongside language analysis. Integrate AO3 context (Windrush generation, 1984 London, racism, cultural displacement) within your analysis, not as a separate paragraph.

Common mistakes to avoid: Plot retelling instead of analysing methods. Bolting context on as a separate paragraph. Forgetting it is a play (not analysing dramatic techniques). Referring to 'Act 1' and 'Act 2' when the play uses scene numbers. Only using examples from one part of the play in a whole-play response. Identifying techniques without explaining their effect on the audience. Always focus on how and why Pinnock presents ideas, not just what happens.

glossary_terms.definition: A sense of fitting in and being accepted within a culture, community or family — the play's central concern.
Having roots in multiple cultures simultaneously, without seeing them as mutually exclusive — Pinnock's most hopeful idea.
The experience of being a mother, including emotional, cultural and practical demands — defined by sacrifice and protectiveness in the play.
The gap in values and worldview between parents and children, often intensified in immigrant families.
Prejudice or discrimination based on race — in Leave Taking, structural and pervasive rather than dramatically staged.
The restoration of family relations without full resolution — Leave Taking's ending is hopeful but not conclusive.
